# Global Supply Chain Resilience & Responsible Sourcing Program
### Multi-Country Direct Materials Network — Board / Executive Committee Decision Document

---

## 0. Executive Summary and Decision Ask

**The problem in one paragraph.** Our sourcing footprint was optimized over fifteen years for landed cost and working capital. It was not designed for shock absorption, and it was not designed for defensible human-rights and environmental due diligence. Both design gaps are now producing measurable cost: unplanned expedite and premium freight, line-down events traceable to sub-tier suppliers we cannot name, and a widening gap between what our Supplier Code of Conduct claims and what we can actually evidence to a regulator, a customer, or an investigative journalist. These are not two problems. They are one problem — inadequate knowledge of, and inadequate leverage over, our extended supply base — expressed in two ways.

**What we recommend.** A three-year, gated, *risk-differentiated* program built on a single principle: **we do not treat all suppliers, parts, or countries the same.** Effort concentrates where criticality and risk intersect. Resilience investment is sized to time-to-recover, not to spend. Ethical due diligence is sized to inherent human-rights risk, not to purchase order value. The two workstreams share one supplier master, one risk score, one governance body, and one set of commercial levers — because splitting them is how organizations end up dual-sourcing into a forced-labour exposure.

**What we are explicitly rejecting.**

| Rejected | Why |
|---|---|
| Blanket dual-sourcing of the whole BOM | Cost and quality dilution with no risk return on 70%+ of parts that are commodity-substitutable inside 30 days |
| "China+1" (or any geography slogan) as a strategy | A second plant in a second country owned by the same parent, feeding from the same sub-tier cluster, is not diversification. Correlation, not geography, is the unit of analysis |
| Audit-count as the ethics KPI | Audit coverage measures our activity, not worker outcomes. Social audits reliably miss forced labour, wage theft, and freedom-of-association violations |
| "Cut and run" on adverse findings | Terminating on discovery transfers harm to workers, destroys the incentive for suppliers to disclose, and leaves us with a supply gap and a worse-informed replacement |
| Buying a control tower platform first | Technology on top of an unmapped, unclean supplier master produces expensive dashboards of wrong data |
| Treating resilience as an inventory question | Inventory is the most expensive and shortest-lived of the seven levers. It buys time to use the other six |

**The decision ask today:**

| Item | Amount (illustrative) | Release trigger |
|---|---|---|
| **Authorize now: Wave 0** — diagnostic, n-tier mapping of critical flows, ethical risk baseline, supplier master remediation, program office, clause library, control-tower architecture & vendor selection | **$4.2M** ($1.1M capex / $3.1M opex), 6 months | — |
| Indicative full-program envelope through Year 3 (planning only, **not** authorized today) | $31M ($9M capex / $22M opex) + $28M one-time working capital for strategic buffers | Each wave released only on written gate closure |
| Recurring run-rate from Year 3 | ~$7.5M p.a. (team, assurance, platform, remediation fund) | Absorbed into category cost-to-serve |
| Expected annual gross margin at risk today (unmitigated) | $95–140M revenue exposure / $38–56M EBIT exposure per major-disruption year | Basis of the business case, re-forecast at each gate |
| Target risk reduction by end Year 3 | ≥60% reduction in Value-at-Risk on Tier-1 critical flows; ≥40% on sub-tier | Independent validation at Gate 3 |

**Answers in one line each:**

1. **Resilience** — segment the base, map to sub-tier where it matters, then apply seven graduated levers (footprint, supplier architecture, buffers, design, contracts, visibility, response capability) differentially by criticality × time-to-recover. §3
2. **Ethics** — move from audit-based compliance to risk-based human-rights due diligence aligned to the UNGP/OECD framework: flow-down standards, unannounced and worker-voice-based assurance, remediation-first response, traceability to the risk point (not just Tier 1), and reform of our own purchasing practices, which currently *cause* some of the violations we audit for. §4
3. **Integration** — one supplier record, one composite risk score, one council, one commercial toolkit; explicit management of the four places where the two agendas conflict. §5–6
4. **Proof** — a 14-metric scorecard split into exposure, capability, and outcome layers, with time-to-recover and worker-outcome measures as the two headline indicators; independent assurance annually. §10

## 0.1 Working Assumptions (Illustrative — Replace With Actuals in Wave 0)

All quantities below are placeholders for scaling the argument. Wave 0's first deliverable is to replace every one of them with measured values.

| Parameter | Assumed value | Source to confirm in Wave 0 |
|---|---|---|
| Direct material spend | $1.4B p.a. | ERP spend cube |
| Active direct suppliers (Tier 1) | ~1,850 | Supplier master (expect 15–25% duplicate/dormant records) |
| Suppliers representing 80% of spend | ~140 | Pareto |
| Suppliers representing 80% of *disruption risk* | Unknown — hypothesis ~350, poorly correlated with spend | Criticality analysis |
| Sourcing countries | 31 | Trade data |
| Countries in top-quartile human-rights risk indices | 11, carrying ~34% of unit volume | ITUC / Global Slavery Index / Freedom House / V-Dem overlay |
| Sole-sourced part numbers | ~2,300 of 11,000 (21%) | PLM + AVL reconciliation |
| Sole-sourced *and* long-qualification (>26 weeks) parts | Hypothesis ~400 — the real problem set | Engineering qualification data |
| Sub-tier visibility (Tier 2+) | <8% of critical flows | Supplier disclosure |
| Average unmitigated time-to-recover, critical single-source node | 14–22 weeks | Historical incidents + supplier survey |
| Average time-to-survive (inventory + alternate capacity coverage) | 5–7 weeks | Inventory + capacity data |
| **Implied structural gap** | **~9–15 weeks of uncovered exposure on critical nodes** | The single most important number in this document |

---

## 1. Diagnostic: Locating Exposure Before Spending on It

Do not skip this. Every failed resilience program we have benchmarked began by buying a solution to an unmeasured problem.

### 1.1 The four-lens exposure model

Assess every critical flow through four independent lenses; risks that appear in more than one lens compound rather than add.

| Lens | Questions | Typical data |
|---|---|---|
| **Node** | Which single facilities, if lost, stop us? Not companies — *facilities*. A multi-plant supplier with one plant making our part is a single node | Supplier plant-level BOM mapping |
| **Network** | Where do independent-looking suppliers converge? Shared sub-tier, shared logistics corridor, shared port, shared specialty chemical, shared foundry, shared certification body | N-tier mapping, trade/bill-of-lading data |
| **Geography** | Natural hazard (seismic, flood, typhoon, drought), political (sanctions, export control, expropriation, conflict), infrastructure (grid, water, port), regulatory (import bans, carbon border levies) | Hazard overlays on plant coordinates |
| **Counterparty** | Financial distress, ownership change, ultimate beneficial ownership, cyber posture, sanctions/PEP exposure, capacity commitments to other customers | Credit data, UBO screening, cyber ratings |

### 1.2 Criticality × substitutability: the segmentation that drives everything

Plot every purchased part (not supplier) on two axes:

- **Impact of loss** — revenue/margin stopped per week, safety or regulatory criticality, customer-specific exposure
- **Time-to-recover (TTR)** — realistic weeks to restore supply from an alternative, including qualification, tooling transfer, certification, and ramp. *Measured, not estimated by the buyer.*

| Segment | Definition | Population (est.) | Resilience posture |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A — Critical / long TTR** | Line-stopping, TTR > 12 wks (tooled, certified, sole-source, specialty material) | ~400 parts / ~90 suppliers | Full treatment: dual qualification or N+1 capacity, strategic buffer sized to TTR gap, contractual capacity reservation, sub-tier mapping to Tier 3, quarterly deep review |
| **B — Critical / medium TTR** | Line-stopping, TTR 4–12 wks | ~1,600 parts | Qualified alternate on paper + tooling escrow/second tool, buffer to 8 wks, annual review |
| **C — Critical / short TTR** | Line-stopping, TTR < 4 wks (fungible commodity) | ~3,000 parts | Approved vendor list ≥3, no dedicated buffer beyond safety stock, market monitoring only |
| **D — Non-critical** | Substitutable or non-line-stopping | Remainder | Standard sourcing; monitor for ethics risk only |

**The key discipline:** capital and management attention flow to Segment A. Roughly 4% of parts should consume ~60% of resilience spend. Any plan that spreads investment evenly is a plan that under-protects A and over-protects D.

### 1.3 Ethical risk heat mapping — a *different* segmentation

Human-rights risk does not correlate with spend or with criticality. It correlates with:

| Driver | Indicators |
|---|---|
| **Sector** | Manual/low-skill labour intensity, seasonal or piece-rate work, hazardous processes, extractives, agriculture, mining, smelting, textiles, electronics assembly, shipbreaking, fishing |
| **Geography** | Weak rule of law, restricted freedom of association, migrant labour corridors, conflict-affected and high-risk areas (CAHRA), state-imposed labour programs, informal economy prevalence |
| **Workforce composition** | Migrant workers (esp. recruited through agencies), contract/agency labour, women in low-tier roles, young workers, home workers |
| **Business model** | Subcontracting depth, unauthorized subcontracting, seasonal surge, short lead times, small suppliers with thin margins |
| **Our own behaviour** | Late order changes, unrealistic lead times, price pressure below cost-of-compliance, long payment terms, cancellation without liability |

The last row deserves emphasis: **a material share of the labour violations found in supply chains is generated by buyer purchasing practices.** Audits find excessive overtime; the overtime exists because we compressed the lead time. Any credible program addresses this or it is theatre.

Score each supplier site 1–5 on inherent risk, then adjust for control maturity. Prioritise **inherent-risk-high sites regardless of spend**, including low-spend and non-critical suppliers.

### 1.4 The joint exposure map

Overlay the two segmentations. Four quadrants, four very different responses:

| | **Low ethical risk** | **High ethical risk** |
|---|---|---|
| **High criticality (Seg. A/B)** | *Standard resilience program.* Dual-qualify, buffer, contract. | **Priority quadrant.** Highest management attention. We cannot easily exit, so we must engage: deep due diligence, on-site presence, capability building, remediation funding, *and* parallel development of an ethically-validated alternate so engagement is a choice, not a hostage position. |
| **Low criticality (Seg. C/D)** | Monitor. | *Rationalise or remediate quickly.* We have exit optionality — but exit responsibly (§4.4), and do not simply push the problem into a less visible supplier. |

The priority quadrant — typically 30–70 supplier sites — is where the program lives or dies.

---

## 2. Design Principles

Ten principles that resolve arguments later:

1. **Segment ruthlessly.** Differentiated treatment by criticality × risk; uniform programs fail on both cost and effect.
2. **Measure resilience as time, not inventory.** The headline metrics are **time-to-recover (TTR)** and **time-to-survive (TTS)**. The objective is TTS ≥ TTR on every Segment A node.
3. **Correlation is the enemy.** Diversify the *risk factor*, not the vendor name.
4. **Redundancy must be exercised.** An unused alternate source degrades to a paper alternate within 18 months. Allocate ≥10% of volume to secondary sources on Segment A parts.
5. **Design is the cheapest lever.** Part standardization and specification flexibility reduce TTR more cheaply than any inventory or dual-tooling strategy — but only on new programs, so start now.
6. **Visibility precedes control, and mapping precedes technology.**
7. **Ethics is due diligence, not audit.** Risk-based, continuous, extending beyond Tier 1, with remediation as the default response.
8. **Leverage is finite; concentrate it.** We have real influence over ~140 suppliers and near-zero over 1,700. Use collective action and industry schemes where we lack unilateral leverage.
9. **Fix our own purchasing practices** as a condition of demanding supplier improvement.
10. **Build the response capability, not just the plan.** Playbooks that have never been exercised do not work at 2 a.m.

---

## 3. Resilience Strategy — Seven Levers

### 3.1 Lever 1 — Footprint and network architecture

| Action | Detail | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| **Regionalization / in-region-for-region** | Target ≥60% of volume for each demand region sourced within that region or a proximate trade bloc, phased over 5 years and applied only where landed-cost penalty < risk-adjusted benefit | New programs first; legacy on natural retooling cycles |
| **Structured near-shore / friend-shore evaluation** | Assess candidate geographies on a 9-factor scorecard: cost, capability, capacity depth, logistics, trade agreement status, political stability, hazard exposure, labour-rights baseline, environmental compliance regime | Segment A/B |
| **Deliberate multi-region redundancy** | For Segment A parts: sources in ≥2 distinct hazard zones, ≥2 distinct political jurisdictions, ≥2 distinct logistics corridors | ~90 suppliers |
| **Manufacture-in-house selectively** | Reserve vertical integration for parts that are simultaneously critical, high-IP, structurally single-source, and volume-stable. Expect 3–5 candidates, not 30 | Case-by-case, Board approval |
| **Logistics diversification** | Alternate ports, second freight forwarder per lane, multimodal options pre-contracted, avoid single-chokepoint routings (canals, straits, single rail corridor) | All inbound lanes >$5M |
| **Trade architecture** | FTA/preferential origin optimisation, bonded and free-trade-zone warehousing for buffer stock, tariff engineering, customs broker redundancy, sanctions and export-control screening automation | Global |

**Realism check:** regionalization is expensive and slow. It should be a *bias applied at natural decision points* (new product introduction, tooling replacement, contract renewal, capacity expansion), not a forced migration program. Forced migrations destroy more value than the disruptions they prevent.

### 3.2 Lever 2 — Supplier base architecture

| Action | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Dual qualification for Segment A** | Not merely "a second name on the AVL." Requires: PPAP/first-article approval complete, tooling available or duplicated, capacity contractually reserved, and a validated production run within the last 12 months |
| **N+1 capacity rule** | Aggregate qualified capacity across the source set ≥ 130% of peak demand for Segment A, ≥ 115% for Segment B |
| **Volume allocation policy** | No single supplier >70% of a Segment A part; secondary source holds ≥10% live volume ("exercise the redundancy") |
| **Tooling and IP control** | Company-owned tooling with title documented and physically tagged; duplicate tools for top-50 parts held at alternate site or in escrow; source code / process recipe escrow for critical proprietary processes |
| **Supplier financial surveillance** | Continuous credit monitoring, Altman-Z-type scoring, payment-behaviour data, plus early-warning behavioural indicators (requests for accelerated payment, key personnel loss, quality drift, delivery variability increase) |
| **Supplier rationalization — carefully** | Consolidation improves leverage and audit coverage but concentrates risk. Rationalise in Segment C/D, *not* Segment A |
| **Sub-tier mandate** | Segment A suppliers contractually required to disclose their own critical sub-tier sources, hold their own dual-source plans, and report their TTR. Audit this claim |
| **Supplier development** | Joint capacity investment, engineering support, lean/quality programs for strategic suppliers where switching is uneconomic |

### 3.3 Lever 3 — Buffers and inventory strategy

Inventory is time you have already bought. Size it to the *gap*, not to a blanket days-of-supply target.

| Buffer type | Design rule |
|---|---|
| **Strategic component buffer** | Segment A only. Volume = (TTR − structural coverage) × weekly consumption × service factor. Held in bonded/FTZ where duty-efficient, geographically separated from the primary plant |
| **Postponement / decoupling** | Hold generic semi-finished inventory at the last common point in the BOM rather than finished goods; increases coverage per dollar dramatically |
